coach_says: Your f6 knight is pinned to your queen by Bg5, and the knight on d7 is the piece holding it together. After b6, White plays Bb5 to hit d7; once that knight is exchanged, Nxf6+ wins material because the d-file opens onto d7 and Bg5 eyes d8. Play a6 first so Bb5 is impossible, or Re8 to give the queen air, before doing anything slow.

Your c6 knight was the only piece guarding e5. Moving it a second time to d4 left the pawn hanging, and Nxe5 wins it while also eyeing f7. In the opening, check what a piece is defending before you move it, and develop a new piece instead of moving the same one twice.

After Nf3 your e5 pawn is attacked, and Bc5 does nothing to defend it, so Nxe5 simply wins a pawn. When your opponent's move attacks something, answer that first: Nc6 or d6 guards e5 and still develops. Bc5 is a fine square, just one move too early.

Three of your pieces were attacked at once (Bb5 by the c6 pawn, Ng5 by h6, Ne4 by Bf5) and ...Nxc2+ was also a threat. Qh5 attacks f7 but defends none of them; Black just takes on g5, and the open h-file then hits your queen. When several pieces are hanging, look for a move that rescues the most, like Bd3, which saves the bishop, guards e4 and covers c2.

Your bishop on d3 has no squares: your own queen on e2 blocks f1 and your c2 pawn blocks the other side. Black was already threatening ...c4, which attacks the bishop and wins it, and Re1 does nothing about that. Play b3 to stop ...c4, and in general don't box a bishop in behind your own queen and pawns.

Your bishop on f4 was attacked by the knight on e6 and nothing defended it. Bb3 goes after d5 but leaves the bishop to be taken for free with Nxf4. Before starting your own attack, check which of your pieces are attacked and undefended: Be5 or Bg3 saves it and keeps your play.

White threatened Qf7 mate: the rook on d7 and queen on e6 both hit f7, and your f6 knight can't help because it is pinned to your king by Rf1. Taking on h2 does nothing about it. Every move, ask what your opponent threatens before you grab material; Qg6 guards f7 and keeps you fine.

You had to block the check, and the choice of blocker mattered. With Rg8 the rook is pinned on the back rank by Re8 and g7 is left empty, so Qf6+ comes in on the long diagonal and it is mate soon after. Bg8 keeps your rook on g7 guarding the king, and White has no more than a draw. When blocking a check, ask which piece you can afford to take off defence.
concept: blocked check with the wrong piece

coach_says: Recapturing on c8 with the queen took away the only defender of your knight on e7, which the rook on e4 was attacking, so Rxe7 wins it. Before recapturing, check what each candidate piece is guarding; Nxc8 recaptures and leaves nothing loose.

White has pushed g4 and wants to attack your king, and g5 helps them: it loosens the pawns in front of your king, leaves holes on f5 and h5, and gives White a target for h4 to open the h-file. When your opponent attacks on one wing, don't push pawns in front of your own king; hit back where they are weak, for example b5 and ...b4 against the queenside.
concept: pushed pawn in front of king

coach_says: f6 opens the diagonal from c4 to your king, so White can play c3 to kick your knight and then Bc4+ with tempo; after ...Nb3 the bishop takes it, and after ...Nf5 Be6 harasses it. Your knight on d4 was your best piece and your rooks were not doing anything. Put a rook on b8 to attack b5 instead of making a pawn move that weakens your king.

Your king is still in the centre and Black's bishop on h6 controls the c1-h6 diagonal. Nc3 took your knight off the defence of d2, so ...Qg5 now aims at d2 and your king gets chased. Play h4 to take g5 away from the queen, or develop the knight to d2 where it still guards that square.

With pawns on e6 and g6, your dark-squared bishop is the piece that covers the holes on f6 and h6. Bh6 offers to trade it, and after Bxh6 Nxh6 your knight sits on the rim and those dark squares have no defender. Put the bishop on g7 or play d6 and keep it.

Your f4 pawn was attacked twice (by g3 and the c1 bishop) and defended only by your queen. Instead of adding a defender, f3 just gives it away and Nxf3 develops White's knight for free. Count attackers and defenders: Bh6 adds a second guard and develops a piece.

Your knight on f3 is pinned to your queen by the bishop on h5. Taking on f6 lets Black recapture with the queen, which then attacks f3 a second time, so you now have to spend moves keeping the knight alive. When a piece is pinned, don't make captures that help your opponent pile on it; Nbd2 or Bxc6+ deals with the pin first.

Bxf6 was strong: the knight on f6 is the only defender of d5, so after Qxf6 you play Nxd5 and win another pawn with tempo on the queen. Bg3 keeps the bishop but lets Black untangle and gives them ...Qb4 against b2. When an enemy piece guards a pawn, ask whether you can trade it off and take the pawn.

The pawn on b5 was free: your bishop on f1 attacks it and nothing of Black's defends it, so Bxb5 just wins a pawn. Instead a4 gives up the a3 pawn's protection of b4, and Nxb4 takes it. Before making a pawn move, check whether there is a loose enemy pawn or piece to take, and what your pawn stops defending.
You were already in trouble here, and d5 and the engine's d6 come to about the same. Both try to free your c8 bishop; there is nothing specific to fix in this move.

Qd3 is about as good as anything else here. The bigger habit to watch is moving your queen three times in the first four moves; getting your knights and bishops out first, for example with Nf3 and g3, saves time.

Your queen was lost whatever you did, but the knight that checked you was not. Rxh2 takes it straight away, and after ...Bxd1 you take back on d1 with the knight and still have Bxa8 coming. After Ke1 the knight escapes via f3 and you end up a full piece worse. When a piece gives check next to your rook, see if you can just take it.
